An environment is a complete, separately governed copy of your model — sources, tables, policies, masking rules and grants. Teams keep a dev environment to change the model in, a staging one to review it in, and prod to serve from, then move the change forward by merging one environment into the next with a diff, an approval and an undoable history.

zh/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.con: per-instance — each instance its own copy

Only matters when Provisa runs as several instances behind a load balancer. It decides whether the materialized view is ONE copy shared by all instances, or a separate copy per instance. Shared: a single copy in the shared store, refreshed by one instance at a time (a short lease with fencing), so every instance reads the same consistent snapshot — pick this when instances must agree. Per-instance: each instance builds and refreshes its own copy independently — simpler and faster, but instances can briefly disagree (eventually consistent), so only safe for a deterministic view over a source that's stable within a refresh cycle. Where the copy lives depends on the federation engine's store: per-instance only makes sense when each instance has its OWN store (e.g. an embedded/in-process DuckDB). With a SHARED external store (Postgres, Trino + object store, a warehouse) every instance writes the same physical table, so use shared — per-instance has nowhere private to write and would just clobber.

The single input delivers the rows that changed (as a delta), and only those rows are merged into the stored table by primary key — so work per refresh scales with the SIZE OF THE CHANGE, not the whole dataset. The cheapest option for large, slowly-changing data. It applies only when all three hold: (1) exactly ONE input (no joins), (2) that input emits a delta — i.e. it runs on a change/CDC signal, not full snapshots, and (3) the view SQL is a plain column projection (no join, filter, GROUP BY, aggregate, DISTINCT, or computed column) so the input's delta maps 1:1 to this view's delta. Also needs a primary key. If a refresh brings no delta (a full-snapshot input or a probe trigger), it falls back to a full recompute for that refresh.

Current state, no history. Every refresh re-runs the whole query and replaces the stored table with the fresh result. Simplest and always correct. Work per refresh scales with the TOTAL size of the inputs, not with how much actually changed.

Current state, no history. Every refresh re-runs the whole query, then merges the result into the stored table by primary key: matching rows are updated in place, new rows inserted, nothing deleted-and-reinserted. The query still recomputes everything, so work scales with total input size — only the write is by key.

zh/tour.json::tour.steps.agricultureReca: You saw the insurer's own data matched by county and crop year to public losses, weather and yields, all in one governed model. One view answers whether the weather explains the losses, in SQL, GraphQL and REST. zh/tour.json::tour.steps.agricultureWeat: NOAA's daily maximum temperature and precipitation for each county, the mean of its reporting stations, over the growing season, May to August: when rain and heat decide the yield.

zh/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingAgent.de: An agent connected over MCP reads the same model. Polly answers this question from the same end-of-day totals the dashboard and BI read, so it names the same branch.
The dashboard is what operations sees. The rest of the tour is back as the administrator, and each statement that follows names the role it runs as.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingAsAnalys: The SQL that follows runs as the bank's reporting analysts. They read the end-of-day totals and the five ledger columns the totals are built from: business date, branch, product, currency and amount. They never see an account, a counterparty or a holder.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingAsOps.de: The next query runs as operations, who drill into postings under the ledger's own rules. They see no posting to a staff account, and every counterparty is withheld.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingAsOpsSql: The explorer now runs as operations, still as recorded at 12 October's close.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingAsReport: As recorded is now set to 1 October's close. A BI tool does the same with SET provisa.as_recorded on its pgwire session. As recorded filters the transactions on updated_at and the daily totals on each day's close, so you see the figures the bank reported that evening.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingAsRestat: As recorded moves to 12 October's close, the last of the thirty days. By then the reversal entered on 6 October and the late trade entered on 7 October have both been recorded.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingChange.d: Suppose volumes outgrow the ledger's compute. Set this table's region to warehouse and its replicate setting to Always, and the ledger is replicated into the warehouse. That is a two-line placement change, and every query, dashboard, BI view and agent answers as before. Built by hand, the same move means new pipelines, a backfill, rewritten aggregation and versioning, repointed reports and a second set of access rules. Then come reconciliation testing, audit and lineage checks, architecture and security review, and a change board. Here the change is a two-line reviewed diff, so testing, audit and architecture review a diff, not a migration.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingChange.t: Changing your mind costs two lines
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingCloses.d: The end-of-day totals are a view materialized in the warehouse on the bank's calendar, which closes at 18:00 London time. The view is one GROUP BY over the ledger's one table, so its build runs whole at the ledger and only the grouped rows come back. It inherits the ledger's versions and needs no history settings of its own. Each day was recorded at its own close. 1 and 2 October were recorded again later, when their restatements arrived.
This works when the ledger's side has the compute to run the end-of-day GROUP BY. Replicating is not free for it either. Every changed row has to be found, read in full and shipped, and aggregating in place is often lighter. With high volumes, reports that read totals and an occasional drill-down, keeping the ledger home tends to win. The declaration lets you choose either way.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingDashboar: London's totals for 1 October, each with the postings behind it nested inside. One request reads the totals from the warehouse and the postings from the ledger, joined along the relationship you just saw.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingDay.desc: 1 October as it stands now. For each branch, product and currency you see what came in, what went out and the net. A BI tool connected over pgwire runs this same SQL.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingJoin.des: Each total carries one key made of its day, branch, product and currency. This relationship follows that key to the postings that carry it, read live from the ledger. The drill-down needs no copy either.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingJoin.tit: From a total to its postings
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingLedger.d: The transaction table is homed in the ledger region and never replicated. No copy of a posting ever lands in the warehouse, and every query over the table runs in the ledger. The end-of-day totals and the drill-downs come off the warehouse's bill, for modest compute in the ledger. Only the totals reach the warehouse, plus the postings a drill-down shows, in passing. The cost is lower and the footprint smaller.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingPostings: London's corporate GBP postings for 1 October, read live from the ledger. The recalled payment appears as its latest version, reversed. Its counterparty is withheld, like every other, and a posting to a staff account would not appear. The ledger's rules apply to the drill-down wherever it is read from.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingRecap.de: The end-of-day totals were computed at the ledger, and the warehouse paid only for what it keeps. The warehouse holds totals and never postings, so there is no second copy of the ledger to govern. The dashboard, BI and the agent read one declared relationship and gave the same numbers. And if keeping the ledger home turns out wrong, a two-line placement change moves it while nothing that reads it changes. Choose lean now: being wrong costs two lines, not a project.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingReported: The corporate totals for 1 and 2 October, as reported at 1 October's close. London's GBP total still carries the payment that was later reversed. 2 October had not closed yet, so it has no figures.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingRestated: The same SQL. London's 1 October total no longer carries the reversed payment, and Edinburgh's 2 October USD total now includes the late trade. The versions reported at each close are kept beside the restated ones, and recorded_at shows when each was recorded.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingScenario: A bank reports its totals at every business day's 18:00 close, and restates a past day when a correction arrives later. The usual way first copies the ledger into the warehouse. This demo does not. Watch four things as you go. What the reporting costs to compute. How much data the warehouse holds, and so how much it must govern. Whether the dashboard, BI and an agent give the same answer. And what it costs to change the decision later.
End-of-day reporting, ledger left in place
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.bankingVersions: The ledger never changes a posting. A correction is a new row with the same transaction id, and it keeps the business date. Three mappings tell Provisa so. The business key is transaction_id, the valid time is business_date and the recorded time is updated_at. Anything built on the table can then be read as of a day, or as it was recorded at a time.
A correction is a new row

zh/tour.json::tour.steps.churnprodJoin.d: This relationship joins each customer to the model's score, so a join over customers scores every one of them.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.churnprodJoin.t: The join that feeds the model
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.churnprodMasked: The scores are the same. The email addresses are masked, because the analyst's mask applies to the list as it applies to the customers' table.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.churnprodNode.d: Here is the same model in JavaScript. Its fitted coefficients were exported from Python, and it is registered as a Node source beside the Python one. Each customer gets the same score from both.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.churnprodPackag: The model's package is a source. It carries the fitted model and a lockfile that pins scikit-learn.
A data scientist's model went to production with no service of its own to run. Its package is pinned. A join feeds its function, which reads as a table, and the masks and row rules every table has govern what it returns. SQL, GraphQL and every other way in read it the same way.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.churnprodRegion: The EU account team looks after the customers billed in the EU.
Now as the EU account team
Only EU customers are listed. The row rule sits on churn_risk itself, and a rule on a code table applies to the rows its code returns.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.churnprodScenar: The churn demo's data scientist trained a scikit-learn model on the customers' usage to find who is about to cancel. Here that model goes to production. It ships as a Python package, and it scores every customer you may see, under the same rules as any table.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.cloudpolicyAppT: The payments team reads its own resources and incidents only.
The same statement returns only the payments team's disks. The row rules sit on the inventory and the incidents, and every view built on them applies them.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.cloudpolicyAudi: The auditor reads every account in every cloud.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.cloudpolicyCite: Each incident cites a policy section. This relationship joins it to the clause it cites, so an incident filed under the wrong section shows up.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.cloudpolicyDash: Superset reads the same views through Provisa's Postgres protocol. Here is its compliance dashboard, with the violations by control.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.cloudpolicyInci: The second source is the security team's ServiceNow incidents. Each one names the disk it is about as its configuration item, and it cites the policy section it is filed under. An exception is an incident in the Policy exception category.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.cloudpolicyMode: Each disk names the machine it is attached to. This relationship joins disks to machines in Azure, AWS and Google Cloud alike.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.cloudpolicyOpen: Here is every disk the review flags, for every team.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.cloudpolicyPoli: Here is every control of the policy, read from its HTML with its heading, its clause and the day it took effect. Section 4.2 is the disk-encryption control under review.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.cloudpolicyPoll: An exception lasts 90 days under section 4.3. Polly finds the disks it still covers.
The policy has controls that no check enforces. Polly compares the policy with the checks the team runs, and it can draft a view for a steward to add.
Polly reads the same governed model you do. It names the disks without a customer-managed key and the section that requires one.
Ask Polly who breaks the control
Some incidents cite a section other than the control they are about, and one cites a section the policy withdrew.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.cloudpolicyRead: The policy itself is a web page. This Python package ships with the page and reads it into a row for each control. Its function is a table, so the policy joins the rest of the model.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.cloudpolicyReca: You reviewed one policy across three clouds from what was already recorded. The policy is a table, read by code from its own page, and each incident joins the clause it cites. A daily trigger keeps the history, and each role reads only what its rules allow, in SQL, in Polly and in Superset.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.cloudpolicyRevi: The daily review classifies each attached disk by the policy's rules. A disk without a customer-managed key may be covered by an exception in date. If it is not, its incident is within its deadline or past it, closed with the disk still not compliant, or never filed.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.cloudpolicyScen: Your security policy says every disk attached to a virtual machine uses a customer-managed key. You lead security, and you review that across Azure, AWS and Google Cloud from what is already recorded. The first source is the cloud inventory. It lists every machine and disk in the three clouds, with the key each disk is encrypted with.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.cloudpolicySear: A search by meaning finds the control about disk encryption even when your words differ from the clause's.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.cloudpolicyTren: The history the trigger keeps shows the violations day by day. Disks drop out as their incidents are fixed, and a new violation shows up the day it appears.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.cloudpolicyTrig: Each morning a scheduled trigger runs the review and writes the day's rows to the review history. It writes through the same governed pipeline as any statement, under its role's write grant.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.cloudpolicyViol: Section 4.2 is written as a view. It lists every attached disk whose key the cloud manages, beside the machine the disk is on.
Orders, revenue and the average order of each segment, by year, from the orders and the customers' segments.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.dataroomAudit.d: Every statement is audited: who ran it, as which role, the tables it read, whether it was answered and how many rows it returned. Here are the statements you just ran as bidder A and bidder B. The seller knows exactly what left the room.
The next statements run as bidder_a, exactly as the analysts' do.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.dataroomBidderB: Bidder B's clean team holds its own role, bidder_b, granted the same room and ending on the same date. Neither bidder sees what the other asks.
Customers who first ordered in the first quarter of 2023, and how many still ordered in each quarter after, with what they spent. Retention, without a single customer.
How many customers each segment and region has, and how many ordered in the last twelve months. A count, never a customer.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.dataroomCrm.des: The sales team's Salesforce: each business customer's account and its deals. Its rows are landed once into the room and read from there, so the bidders' questions never reach Salesforce.
The Users page lists each grant with its end date and its last use. After the deal date the grants are gone, removed by the schedule and recorded in the org's trail, and nothing more leaves the room.
Access ends on the deal date
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.dataroomGrant.d: Each analyst's grant of bidder_a carries an end date: the deal date. From that moment the role is no longer theirs, on every request however it arrives. An account has no end date of its own; the grant's end ends the access.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.dataroomGrant.t: A grant that ends on the deal date
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.dataroomIntro.d: Northfield Supply is selling itself, and each prospective buyer's clean team needs to see the business before it bids. Instead of exporting extracts into a data room, the seller connects Provisa to its own systems and gives each bidder governed access that ends on the deal date. Nothing is copied out, and no customer identity leaves the room. This is the order and finance system, a Postgres database read in place: 2,400 customers, their orders since 2023 and the invoice of each.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.dataroomIntro.t: A data room with no exports
On the seller's Users page, bidder A's two analysts are added as local accounts, each bound to the bidder_a role. They sign in to the seller's Provisa over HTTPS. A self-hosted seller exposes only HTTPS, through its own TLS edge (an ingress or reverse proxy with a public certificate), while the stores, the engine and the database protocols stay private; on hosted Provisa the org's own address already serves it. Nothing in this demo opens a port.
Setting up the room: invite the analysts
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.dataroomPipelin: The CRM's deals by industry and stage, with their value and their value weighted by the chance each closes. The businesses' and the deals' names stay in the CRM.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.dataroomProfile: Each column of the invoices table as the profiler found it: its rows, nulls, distinct values and range. A bidder learns how complete the records are without reading one of them. Here, some invoices have never been paid.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.dataroomQuality: Each check of the seller's records and how many rows fail it: customers with no email, phone numbers that are not ten digits, invoices never paid. The flaws a buyer looks for, counted.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.dataroomRecap.d: A data room with no exports: the seller's own systems, read in place, shown to each bidder as aggregates, profiles, quality scores, masked samples and records without identities. No customer identity leaves the room. Each bidder holds a role of its own, granted until the deal date, and every statement is audited.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.dataroomRefused: Bidder A asks for the customers' names. Provisa refuses: no customer name is granted to bidder_a, and neither are the CRM's business and deal names. Had the analyst named bidder B's role, which they do not hold, the request would be refused too, and recorded in the org's security trail as role probing.
A bidder that drops out loses access in one action: remove its grant, or the role itself. The next request is refused. The audit of everything it read stays.
Ending a bidder's access at once
One customer in fifty, as a bidder reads them: no name, the email's name part and the phone's digits masked. The shape of the data, never the person.
The seller acts as every role it holds again, to see what the bidders did.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.dataroomSignedI: Signed in, an analyst of bidder A sees what bidder_a is granted: the aggregate views, the profiles, the masked sample and the seller's records without a single customer identity. No customer's name, and no business or deal name from the CRM, is there to read.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.datavaultAnalys: Next, the SQL explorer runs as the European analyst. Personal data lives in the satellites, so that's where it's governed.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.datavaultAnswer: The answer, in one point-in-time query. For each date on which anything about the customer was loaded, you see the version of each system's values in force at that time, and since when. From 1 September to 15 November, the two systems disagreed about where the customer lived.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.datavaultArrive: Every row either system received for Alfreds Futterkiste. The order system heard of its move on 1 September 1997; the CRM sent the old address again on 1 October, and the move on 15 November.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.datavaultCrm.de: The CRM holds the same customers as accounts, with each contact's email, which the order system never had. Its addresses can differ from the order system's, and for a while they do.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.datavaultGraphq: The business vault view is a GraphQL field too, filtered to the customer and ordered by time.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.datavaultHub.de: One row for each customer either system knows. Each row has the customer's code, the hash key of that code (which every link and satellite joins on), the system the customer was first seen in, and when.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.datavaultInsert: The customer table is insert-only, as a vault's staging receives it: a change arrives as a new row with its load date, and nothing is overwritten.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.datavaultLineag: The lineage of the mart's columns: each one traced back through the point-in-time view and the satellites to the source field it came from.
Where a mart column comes from
Links pair the hubs' hash keys: a customer placed an order, an order contains a product. The relationships between them let GraphQL and Cypher walk the vault from hub to link to hub.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.datavaultMasked: As the analyst, the CRM satellite shows only European customers. Their contacts are withheld, and the names in their emails and the digits of their phone numbers are hidden. The hubs and links stay readable, so the analyst can still join on them.
Masked where the personal data is
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.datavaultProduc: The product satellite keeps Chai's old name beside Chai Tea, and Chang's price before and after its correction.
A renamed product, a corrected price
Two live systems and a data vault over them, declared as views: hubs, links and satellites with every version kept, refreshed by the engine as rows arrive, governed in the satellites, and queried point-in-time in SQL, GraphQL and REST, with lineage back to the source fields. No separate ETL platform, job server or pipeline code.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.datavaultRest.d: The current-state customer dimension, built on the vault, is a REST endpoint: a downstream application reads it without knowing the vault is there.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.datavaultSatell: A satellite keeps each system's attributes for the customer. Every version is a row, with its load date and a hashdiff over its values. The CRM's resend on 1 October has the same hashdiff as the row before it, so it doesn't count as a new version.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.datavaultScenar: An order system and a CRM, both from Northwind, each keep their own copy of every customer. The question: what did we know about this customer, from which source, and when? A data vault answers that by keeping every version from every source. Here the vault is declared as views, and the engine builds and refreshes it. There's no ETL platform, job server or pipeline code to run. The work runs on the engine, where it scales, and one declared vault feeds the marts, the governed APIs and the lineage.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.datavaultWalk.d: Hub to link to hub: the customer, its orders, the products in them, and every version of each product's name and price.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.filesAnswer.des: The stored view complaints_near_construction counts, for each neighborhood, the complaints made at an address with an active permit. Look at which neighborhood comes first.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.filesComplaints: complaints is one table over every file named complaints_*.csv in the folder. Each month's file is part of it; a new month's file needs no table of its own.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.filesDone.descr: A folder of files became a governed catalog: tables, relationships, an ontology term and a stored view, with nothing loaded. A new month's complaints file needs no new table: the glob already names it.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.filesDone.title: A folder became a catalog
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.filesFormats.de: building_permits is read from a Parquet file, as the budget is from an Excel workbook and the inspections from a JSON file. Each is a governed table like any other.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.filesIntro.desc: A city publishes its open data as files: 311 complaints in a CSV file a month, building permits in Parquet, the budget in Excel and inspections in JSON. drop is one files source over that folder: every file is a table, read where it lies, with no load step. The question: which neighborhoods have the most complaints near active construction?
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.filesJoin.descr: The relationship DRAWS joins a building permit to the complaints made at its address. The view that answers the question joins along it.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.filesJoin.title: Complaints at permitted addresses
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.filesMonths.des: The complaints counted by month: each month comes from its own file, read as one table. Look for one row for each monthly file.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.filesRest.descr: The same view as a REST call. Every table and view is served over REST, GraphQL and SQL alike, under the same rules.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.filesRest.title: The same answer over REST
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.filesTerm.descr: The ontology says what an open complaint is: one the city has not yet closed. Terms like this say what the catalog's data means.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.filesTerm.title: What an open complaint is
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.hasuramigration: BUYS_FOR joins a customer to their Salesforce account, approved like the relationships the import carried. From here the account is one field away from every customer, in every interface, under every role's rules.
One more relationship

Analysts can read order totals and account links, but no names or emails, and never cancelled orders. Those are the row rule and column lists the import carried over. Next, the role picker switches to analyst.
The analyst

Ana is a customer. Her token carried x-hasura-user-id: 1, and Provisa reads that claim as the session value hasura_user_id, which the imported row rules compare against. Next, the role picker switches to ana, so the queries below run just as the storefront runs them for her.
Signed in as Ana
Support staff can read every order and every customer, as their Hasura permissions allowed. Next, the role picker switches to support, and the support desk's order screen runs as they run it.
The support desk

One SQL statement over the store and Salesforce: revenue by the industry of the account behind each order. The analyst's rules apply as they do in GraphQL: cancelled orders are left out, and no name or email is read.
Revenue by industry

Admin › Import read the app's Hasura metadata export and showed what it became before applying anything. Carried as it is: the tables, their custom names, every relationship, the select, insert, update and delete permissions as row rules, column grants and write grants. Mapped to a better Provisa feature, each saying why: the inherited role, the action as a command, the event trigger as a trigger on the table's changes, the session variable and the claim that supplies it. Redo by hand, each saying what to do: the computed field and the trigger retries.
One import, and it works

The storefront's order-history query, reshaped once for Provisa: the root field carries its domain, the column names follow Provisa's convention, and order_by is a list. The relationships items and product kept their Hasura names. Run as Ana, it answers her four orders and no one else's.
The order history, reshaped

Hasura's customers_by_pk becomes a filter on the table. The full_name computed field is just the two names the screen puts together, and the import listed it as one to redo by hand. The row rule still decides what Ana sees: only her own row.
A read by key

A Hasura app imported in one step and working at once: tables, names, relationships, roles, row rules, write permissions, the action and the triggers. The queries changed shape once; the rules did not change at all. And one relationship later, the app reads its Salesforce accounts beside its orders, with nothing to keep in sync.
What you saw
The sales team keeps its accounts in Salesforce. Provisa registers the org as a source and its Account object as a table. Each business customer in the store names the account it buys for.
What Hasura couldn't do: Salesforce

An outfitter's storefront and support desk ran on Hasura v2 over this PostgreSQL database: customers, the catalog, orders and their lines, with roles for customers, support staff and analysts. The team moves the app to Provisa, and gains what Hasura could not give it: the sales team's Salesforce accounts beside the orders, under the same rules.
An app moving off Hasura

The support desk's order screen, reshaped, with something new: beside each order's customer, the account from Salesforce, its industry and city, in the same request. Customers without an account show none.
Orders with their accounts

The four tables came over with the names the app uses. customers keeps Hasura's custom names givenName and familyName, the products table keeps its root name catalog, and each column carries the roles that may read it, from the select permissions.
The tables, as the app knew them
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderAsContro: Next, the SQL explorer runs as every role again.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderAsReview: Next, the SQL explorer runs as reviewer_ben, the first-level reviewer of the trading, research and operations desks.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderAudit.de: ops.queries records every statement: who ran it, as which role, over which table. The reviewer's reads of the queue and the watch list are here, as are yours.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderCustomer: The same mail is checked for customer data by SQL patterns: social security and account numbers. The customer table's columns are tagged pii, so this read is itself recorded.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderDone.des: Watch-list deals were matched against outbound mail by name and by meaning, ranked for review, and the list itself was never shown to the reviewer. This is post-review analytics behind real-time controls, not a replacement for data-loss prevention. Attachments, images, encoded text and personal channels are outside it. Monitoring employees needs disclosure and, in places, a works-council agreement.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderDone.tit: What this is, and is not
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderIntro.de: Northgate Partners, an invented bank, keeps a watch list of the deals it is working on. The question: is anyone sending deal-sensitive or customer data out of the bank? bank is its database: the watch list, the employees and their mail, and the customers and who read their records. Every name and record here is generated.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderLeak.des: Two of the messages behind the queue. A trader not on deal Falcon tells a personal address about it in his own words, with no name, ticker or code name, and it ranks near the top. The deal team's mail to the deal's counsel names everything, and ranks low.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderLeak.tit: A paraphrase outranks the expected mail
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderMail.des: message holds the employees' outbound mail: who sent it, when, and how many recipients were outside the bank or at a personal address.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderMatch.de: deal_match is what the match_deals command found: for each message and deal, whether it names the company, an alias, the ticker or the code name, and how close it reads to the deal's description through a local embedding model. A paraphrase that avoids every name still scores.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderOverTheW: Who was brought over the wall for the deal, and so who could have known of it. The flagged sender is not among them.
Was the sender over the wall?
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderPiiAcces: ops.pii_access lists every read of a pii-tagged table: here, the read you just made. The queue does the same for the bank's staff from the bank's own access log: the operations employee who read customer records that week and then mailed customer data out ranks first.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderQueue.de: One materialized view ranks every case. The match is weighted by context: a sender outside the deal's team, a recipient outside the bank or at a personal address, and a message sent before the announcement raise it; a deal-team member writing to the deal's own counterparties lowers it.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderReviewer: The same queue, read as the reviewer: only the cases of the desks they review, the flagged entity shown and the deal withheld. Row rules on the mail and its matches do this; nothing is copied. The watch list itself is refused to them.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderWatchLis: deal is the control room's watch list: each deal's company, the names it goes by, its ticker, its project code name and whether it is public yet. It is the most restricted table here: the control room reads it, a deal team only its own deal, and a first-level reviewer never.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderWhyFlagg: Polly helps the human reviewer after the fact. Its answer was made when the demo was built, and is shown as stored.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.insuranceAnswer: The view exposure_by_county joins the book to the risk in each county, and is kept stored. Ordered by insured value weighted by risk percentile, it puts the counties where the most exposure meets the highest risk first.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.insuranceBook.d: Each policy in force: its county, line of business, total insured value, premium and deductible.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.insuranceByRati: The same view grouped by FEMA's risk rating: how much of the book's insured value sits in counties rated Relatively High or Very High.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.insuranceGovdat: The government data comes from AskAmerica.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.insuranceJoin.d: The book and the public risk tables share the county's FIPS code, and these relationships join them. Every query that crosses them uses this join.
You saw the insurer's own data joined by county to public risk data, all in one governed model. One view answers where the exposure meets the risk, in SQL, GraphQL and REST, and each role sees only what it's allowed to.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.insuranceRest.d: The view is a REST endpoint too, grouped and summed on the server. Any client that speaks HTTP gets the answer without writing SQL.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.insuranceRisk.d: Every US county's all-hazard risk score and rating, its national percentile, its expected annual loss and the value of all its buildings. The wildfire and storm tables sit beside it.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.insuranceScenar: A property insurer wants to know where its exposure is concentrated against natural-hazard risk. Its own book of policies, with the total insured value of each, is in its database; the hazard risk of every US county is public, in FEMA's, the US Forest Service's and NOAA's data. The tour shows Provisa joining the two, by county, and answering the question in SQL, over REST and in GraphQL.
The ontology names what an underwriter asks about: total insured value, accumulation, probable maximum loss and expected annual loss. Here, accumulation means exposure concentrated where one event can reach many policies.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.opioidsAllocati: Every allocation the fund made: the county, the fiscal year, the program area, the provider paid, what was awarded and what has been spent. Staff see every row; the public role sees none.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.opioidsAnswer.d: The view treatment_against_burden joins the fund's treatment and recovery spending to each county's deaths, and is kept stored. Ordered by deaths for each million dollars spent, it puts the counties where the money meets the most deaths first.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.opioidsAsPublic: The SQL explorer now runs as the public role, the role the council's dashboard and residents use. The statements that follow see only what it allows.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.opioidsByRegion: The dashboard grouped by the fund's five regions: how many residents each has, and how much treatment and recovery was spent there.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.opioidsDeaths.d: Overdose deaths per 100,000 residents in each county in 2023. Where a county had 1 to 9 deaths, CDC suppresses the count and publishes a modelled rate instead, flagged here, so every county has a rate to compare.
The government data comes from AskAmerica: CDC's overdose deaths and death rates, the Census Bureau's population and USAspending's federal spending, each by county.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.opioidsJoin.des: The fund's counties and the public tables share the county's FIPS code, and these relationships join them. Every query that crosses them uses this join.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.opioidsPublic.d: The council's dashboard, run as the public role: the view overdose_burden_by_county. It shows each county's residents, deaths, death rate and federal money per resident, and reads none of the fund's allocations or the providers paid.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.opioidsRecap.de: The fund's own records and public health and census data, joined by county in one governed model. Two stored views answer the question: the staff's, which reads the fund's spending, and the public's dashboard, which reads none of it. Each is served in SQL, GraphQL and REST to the roles allowed to read it.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.opioidsRest.des: The view is a REST endpoint too, grouped and summed on the server, so a council website or a spreadsheet can read the dashboard over HTTP.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.opioidsScenario: A state opioid settlement fund pays Ohio's 88 counties for treatment, recovery, prevention and naloxone. The council asks which counties have the most overdose deaths for the treatment the money pays for. The fund's allocations are in its own database; deaths, population and federal spending are public. The fund and its figures are made up; the counties and the public data are real.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.opioidsTerms.de: The ontology explains the terms a council member or a resident will meet: settlement fund, abatement, allocation, expenditure, suppressed count and rate per 100,000. Here, abatement means what the settlements require the money to be spent on.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.pharmaAnswer.de: The view product_risk joins each product's stock to its shortage, its manufacturer's ongoing recalls and its Medicaid prescriptions, and is kept stored. The critical products at risk come first, fewest days of supply first.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.pharmaByRisk.de: The same view grouped by risk: how many products face a shortage, a recall or both, the stock they hold and how often Medicaid prescribes them.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.pharmaFormulary: Each product the pharmacy stocks: its NDC, generic name, manufacturer, therapeutic class and whether it is critical. Its stock at each site sits beside it.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.pharmaGovdata.d: The government data comes from AskAmerica.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.pharmaJoin.desc: The formulary meets the shortages and Medicaid's prescriptions by NDC. A recall names its firm, not its NDC, so the vendor master records each manufacturer's FDA firm name, and this relationship joins it to the recalls.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.pharmaJoin.titl: Joined by NDC and by firm
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.pharmaRecap.des: You saw the pharmacy's own data joined by NDC and by firm to public drug data, all in one governed model. One view answers which products are at risk, in SQL, GraphQL and REST, and each role sees only what it's allowed to.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.pharmaRest.desc: The view is a REST endpoint too, grouped and summed on the server. Any client that speaks HTTP gets the answer without writing SQL.
A hospital pharmacy wants to know which of its products face shortage or recall risk. Its formulary and the stock each site holds are in its own database; FDA's drug shortages and recalls and Medicaid's prescriptions are public. The tour shows Provisa joining the two and answering the question in SQL, GraphQL and REST.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.pharmaShortages: Every shortage FDA has posted, one row per package: its status, the product's availability and its NDC product code. The recalls and Medicaid's prescriptions sit beside it.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.pharmaTerms.des: The ontology names what a pharmacy buyer asks about: NDC, formulary, drug shortage, recall class and days of supply. Here, supply risk means a shortage, a recall by the product's maker, or too few days of stock on hand.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingAnswer: The view customer_columns keeps each customers column as the latest run found it, emptiest first. A fifth of the customers never answered the marketing question; some emails are missing and some hold a name instead; signup dates start at a 1900-01-01 placeholder, and lifetime values run from refunds below zero to test accounts at 999,999.99.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingCountr: The five most common values in the country column. US, USA and United States are one country, written three different ways in just these five. A count by country would split it into three.
Setup ran the profiler twice, and between the runs the CRM's next sync wrote every US postal code as ZIP+4. The drift table compares each measure with the previous run's: the measures postal_code's change moved are flagged drifting, and the columns the sync left alone are not.
What changed since the last run
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingDuplic: The model declares customer_id the key, but the export held no constraint: 150 customers are in it twice, every field the same. The profile counts the repeated rows and the key values held by more than one row.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingMember: The customers and orders tables are members of the profiler. From a member's editor you can run a profile at once or view its runs: each run, its rows and how long it took.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingOrigin: Ten customers as the CRM holds them. Next, the same statement in an environment generated from the profile.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingPhones: Each phone number reduced to its shape: a digit becomes 9. The CRM never checked the format, so one column holds four of them, which a join or a dialer would have to reconcile first.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingProfil: A profiler holds a schedule and its run settings, nothing else: this one runs every night at 02:00. Its first run was made when the demo was built, so the results are already here.
You saw the acquired company's tables and a profile of them made by the built-in profiler and kept as governed tables. Nulls, ranges, formats, plausible types and duplicates each answer what is actually in this data, in SQL, GraphQL and REST, and each role sees only what it's allowed to.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingRest.d: The view is a REST endpoint too. A data quality tool or a migration script gets the profile without writing SQL.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingRuns.d: A run's results land as tables of their own, one for each kind of measure, and every run is kept beside the ones before it. Here are the customers table's runs, with the rows each read and the repeated rows it found.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingScenar: An outdoor retailer has bought a smaller one, Harbor Outfitters, and received its CRM's customers and orders. Before anyone builds on them, the question is: what is actually in this data? Provisa's built-in Data Profiler answers it, and its results are governed tables like any other, read in SQL, GraphQL and REST.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingStrata: postal_code in each run, the oldest at the back: the share of rows each value holds. The newest run is flagged as drifting, as the drift table showed, and the run before it is not.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingSynthe: The same statement in synthetic: every row generated from the customers' profile, with the same columns, value shapes and spread, and none of the real customers. The profile is enough to generate test data from.
The ontology defines data profile, plausible type, value shape, duplicate row and placeholder value, and ties each term to the measures it describes.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingTerrai: Opening the customers table's profile runs on the terrain
The latest run of customers, drawn as terrain: one ridge for each column, its height the rows in each range of values, and each column's nulls in front of it.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingToProd: Next, the switcher returns to prod.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingToSynt: Next, the switcher moves to synthetic, a Test (synthetic) environment.
The profile infers what a column holds from its values, its name and its tags: an email, a phone number, a postal code, an identifier. Each comes with its confidence and the evidence for it.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.provisioningAsD: Now as the data science role, whose feature store needs the orders but not the margins.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.provisioningAsF: The SQL explorer now runs as the finance role, the team that reads margins in full.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.provisioningClo: close_by_category, finance's close, may be read only from 02:00 to 02:15 UTC. Outside it this read is refused, naming the view and when its window next opens.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.provisioningDat: The same dataset, the same query: cost and margin read 0, and service orders are gone (a row rule). One dataset, two governed views, no copies.

order_margins has every order with its revenue, cost and margin. It keeps every version of every row, so a team can read it as of any moment, and that's what a team pulls. Its load window says when users and clients may read it. Here that's all day except 00:00 to 00:30 UTC. A real warehouse would usually open a narrower overnight window; the demo's is wide so you can walk through it at any hour.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.provisioningFee: Orders arrive on Kafka a few a second, after a month of history; prices and stock counts on their own topics. Each lands into the warehouse's own table within seconds, and each landing refreshes the datasets built on it.
The feeds, landed as they arrive
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.provisioningFin: The latest orders as finance reads them: revenue, cost and margin, every category.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.provisioningJoi: An order names its product, and the product knows its cost and category. The dataset joins each order to its product. The close is built on the dataset plus the stock and price feeds: a view over a view, refreshed in turn.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.provisioningNot: Inside the window a scheduled trigger writes a notice for each team: finance every five minutes, data science two minutes later. The notices table's live Kafka output publishes each to the topic dataset-ready. The notice's time is the dataset's version time.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.provisioningPul: Each team's consumer reads the notice and pulls the whole dataset over Arrow Flight as recorded at its version time: the orders that had landed by then, so neither a refresh landing mid-pull nor an order landed later can change what it reads. It records the rows, the seconds and the rows a second.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.provisioningRec: Feeds landed as they arrived, and datasets were built and refreshed from them. Each team was told on Kafka when a dataset was ready, and pulled it over Arrow Flight as of that moment, seeing only what its role allows and only inside the dataset's window. No copies, and no extraction jobs.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.provisioningRes: How each team's pulls went, grouped on the server: how many, and how fast on average.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.provisioningSce: A coffee roaster's warehouse takes three feeds (orders, prices and stock counts) and builds datasets from them as they land. Two teams downstream need the big one, every order with its margin: finance for its reporting, data science for its feature store. The question: how do they get it as soon as it is ready, without copying it or writing extraction jobs?
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.provisioningWar: Its products and what each costs, the notices it sends when a dataset is ready, and the pulls the teams' consumers record.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.qualityAdmitted: Every silver row carries the run id of the checks that admitted its batch. The relationship ADMITTED_BY joins it to those checks in dq_results.
From a row to the checks that admitted it
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.qualityBronze.d: bronze holds every batch as it landed, never changed. Clean data is typed on landing: the sale id, when it was sold, the quantity. The messy fields, shop code, product and price, stay raw until silver.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.qualityBronze.t: Bronze: typed where it is clean
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.qualityChecks.d: dq_results is a materialized view that computes the checks in SQL on every landed batch: how many rows fail each, and pass or fail. Batch 1 passes them all; batch 2 fails three.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.qualityDone.des: Landing a batch refreshed the checks, silver and gold, and nothing else had to run. The clean batch reached gold. The bad one stopped at bronze, and you can find out why with a query.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.qualityGold.des: Gold is one GROUP BY over silver: sales, items, revenue and the price range by day and product, from checked data only.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.qualityIntro.de: A chain of five shops sends its sales as a daily feed. Each batch lands as the bronze layer in sales, the chain's database. Everything after bronze is a materialized view (the checks, silver and gold), and landing a batch is enough to refresh them all. The question: can I trust this data before it reaches gold?
Gold, silver and the checks are one data product: the totals consumers read, the sales behind them, and the evidence each batch passed. Bronze stays out.
A data product to hand on
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.qualityRaw.desc: The products of the first batch as they landed: one product in several spellings, such as COFFEE, Coffee and cofee. Silver makes them one.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.qualityRaw.titl: Raw, as the feed spelled it
The rows of batch 2 that fail a check, still in bronze as they landed: a shop the chain does not have, negative quantities, prices that are not numbers. None of batch 2 reaches silver; batch 1 stays.
What the bad batch failed on
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.qualitySilver.d: Silver is bronze cleaned up, built only from the batches that passed. Shop codes are trimmed and upper-cased, each product has one spelling, the price is a number, the day is worked out, and a sale sent twice is kept once, in its latest version.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.qualityWhichChe: A silver sale and, along ADMITTED_BY, every check of the run that admitted it: each one passed, with no failing rows.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.reproduceAsFile: This is the time the report was first built and filed, taken from the answer in the refreshes step. It falls after the filed figures were entered and before the correction was. The report is now read as Provisa had it recorded at that time, so nothing recorded later can change it.
As recorded when it was filed
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.reproduceAsOf.d: The report as of its business date: what the figures were for 30 September.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.reproduceAsOfNo: Read as Provisa has it recorded today, 30 September shows the corrected figure: 1,550,000 for the rates desk. That is what the books say now, not what was filed.
As of 30 September, as recorded now
The audit log records every read: who ran it, as which role, and the time it read the report as of and as recorded at. The regulator's reproduction is itself on record.
Who read it, and as of when
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.reproduceBook.d: Each position: its desk, its notional in its own currency and the rate it converts to USD at, valid from 30 September. One of these rates is corrected after the report is first filed.
As of 30 September and as recorded when it was filed: the rates desk reads 1,540,000, the figure the regulator received. The correction recorded since does not change what was filed.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.reproduceImpact: Rename fx_rate here, and Provisa lists what reads it before you save: the report among them. Nothing that depends on a column changes without being named first.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.reproduceLineag: The report's exposure column, traced back: each desk's exposure is the sum of notional times fx_rate over its positions. Every column of the report leads to the source columns it is computed from.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.reproduceNow.de: Each desk's exposure as the report stands today, with when Provisa recorded each figure. The rates desk reads 1,550,000: the corrected rate.
One report, explained and reproduced: its figure traced to its source columns and the refresh that built it, the impact of a change named before it is made, the report as filed beside the report now, and every read of it in the audit log.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.reproduceRefres: Each build of the report records what it was built from: the version of the report's definition, and the version of its input with how that was established. Two builds: one as first filed, one after the correction.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.reproduceScenar: A bank files an exposure report with its regulator for 30 September. The regulator asks where the rates desk's figure came from, and for the report exactly as it was filed: a rate has been corrected since. The bank's trading book is read live from its own database.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.retailAccess.de: Everything the group holds about the person behind each access request, from both subsidiaries, in one query. Amélie Fournier is a member in the EU and in the US.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.retailAsAdmin.d: Next, the SQL explorer runs as every role again.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.retailAsAnalyst: Next, the role picker switches to group_analyst, who works on group reporting in the US, so the SQL and GraphQL after this run as group_analyst.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.retailAsDpo.des: Next, the SQL explorer runs as dpo, who answers data subject requests.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.retailAsEuRevie: Next, the SQL explorer runs as reviewer with region__eu: a reviewer whose region is the EU.
As a reviewer in the EU
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.retailAsMarketi: Next, the SQL explorer runs as marketing_eu.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.retailAsReviewe: Next, the SQL explorer runs as reviewer, the group's insider review.
EU marketing reads the EU customers who agreed to marketing, and only them. The view is built in the EU from EU rows.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.retailAudit.des: Every statement the tour ran: who ran it, on what, and which region answered it. One audit trail across both regions.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.retailErasure.d: For each erasure request, every row the group deletes: its subsidiary, its table and its key. Each subsidiary deletes its own rows, in its own region.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.retailEuCustome: The EU customers. The table names the EU as its region: its rows are copied only into the EU's store and computed only there. Readers elsewhere get them through the EU's views or not at all.
An EU table, homed in the EU
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.retailEveryRole: Next, the role picker switches back to All.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.retailGroupGrap: The same group view over GraphQL: one model, every transport, the same rules.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.retailGroupView: Every loyalty customer of the group. US customers appear as they are; EU customers appear by a pseudonym the EU computed, with no name or address. The EU part was read from the EU's store, and the record of this query names the EU as the region that answered.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.retailJoin.desc: A request joins to each subsidiary's customers by email address. That is how one request finds the same person in both.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.retailJoin.titl: How a request finds a person
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.retailLimits.de: These features can support meeting the GDPR's rules on where data lives and who reads it, but they do not make a group compliant. That takes active design by people who know the data protection and cross-border transfer rules that apply. The lawful basis, the impact assessment, retention and any works-council agreement remain the group's own legal process.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.retailLimits.ti: What this is, and is not
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.retailQueue.des: EU staff's outbound mail, scored in the EU: a personal address, customer records attached, a bulk export. The queue carries the score, the signals and a pseudonym of the sender. No message text leaves the EU, and the sender is withheld.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.retailRecap.des: One model defined both regions: where each table lives, which views are built where, and who reads what. Group reporting read EU customers pseudonymised, EU marketing read only consenting customers, and a request for access and an erasure were each one query. The insider review revealed a sender only in the EU, and every read is in one record.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.retailRegions.d: The US subsidiary's database, homed in the US. The model declares both regions and says, once, where every table lives and which views are built where. A second Provisa node runs in the EU: it copies the EU tables into the EU's own store and builds the EU views there. You are on the US node, which reads EU data only from that EU store, so every cross-border rule is applied in one place.
The group's register of requests: who asked to see their data, who asked to have it erased, and when. It holds no customer data itself.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.retailReveal.de: The same queue. The sender column's mask list reveals the sender only to a reviewer who also holds region__eu; everyone else reads it withheld. It is one grant, reviewer and region__eu, with no role made for the combination.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.retailReveal.ti: The sender, revealed in the EU
A retail group runs an EU and a US subsidiary as one business. Can it do that without breaking GDPR? Each subsidiary keeps its own database: this is the EU one, with its loyalty customers, their marketing consent, orders, staff and the mail staff send outside the group.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.reviewsBatteryD: The shop's first question, in SQL: the reviews that say "battery dies", counted by product, with each product's ratings. One statement reads an Elasticsearch search and two MongoDB tables, and a handful of products stand out.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.reviewsBoughtWi: The second question, in Cypher: the products rated under three stars, and what their buyers also bought. The graph runs across the MongoDB ratings and the Neo4j purchases, and power banks keep turning up.

The same result, grouped by degree to answer the question it was drawn for. The groups bring out the products most often bought together with the low-rated ones, and a bigger number means more pairings run through that product. Degree is counted within this result only: the products rated under three stars, and what five or more of their customers also bought. The red nodes are the products. The ratings and the pair nodes are grouped too.
We can graph it. But what does it mean?
An electronics shop wants to know which products disappoint, and what their buyers do about it. The answer is spread over three NoSQL stores. This one, catalog, is MongoDB: a document for each product, its specs nested, and the star ratings customers give.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.reviewsCypherTa: bought_together is a Cypher query against Neo4j, registered as a table: for each product, every other product its buyers bought, and how many of them did.
A Cypher query as a table
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.reviewsDone.des: Three NoSQL stores, a MongoDB pipeline, an Elasticsearch search and a Cypher query, joined on the product and asked the shop's question in SQL, Cypher, REST and GraphQL.
An example query: the battery complaints in GraphQL, each review's highlighted text with its product nested beneath it through the relationship.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.reviewsGraphSto: purchases is Neo4j: 2,000 customers, each linked by a BOUGHT relationship to the products they bought. All three stores name a product by the same id.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.reviewsJoin.des: Relationships join the tables on the product id across all three stores. COMPLAINS_ABOUT joins a matching review to its product in the catalog, so a query reaches from Elasticsearch to MongoDB without spelling out the join.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.reviewsPipeline: ratings_by_product is a MongoDB aggregation pipeline, registered as a table: it groups the star ratings by product and gives each product's count, average and one-star ratings. A query reads it like any other table.
A MongoDB pipeline as a table
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.reviewsRest.des: The same search as a REST call, its phrase passed as a parameter. Every surface Provisa serves reads the same governed tables, so REST answers as SQL and GraphQL do, under the same rights.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.reviewsSearchSt: reviews is Elasticsearch: the 5,000 reviews customers wrote, each with its product, its stars and its text.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.reviewsSearchTa: reviews_matching is an Elasticsearch search, registered as a table. Its phrase is a parameter: a query sets it, and each row is a review whose text holds the phrase, with the phrase highlighted.
An Elasticsearch search as a table
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.sonnetsDone.des: Shakespeare's lines went from Postgres rows to Qdrant vectors, governed searches and a graph of echoes and themes.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.sonnetsEchoNetw: The echo network, drawn by Cypher: the lines that closely echo a line of another sonnet, and the sonnets they are in. Look for the sonnets joined by more than one echo.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.sonnetsEchoes.d: The echo table. The command link_echoes asks the vector store for each line's three nearest lines in other sonnets and writes them here, each with its similarity.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.sonnetsGraph.de: Three relationships make the tables a graph: a line is IN its sonnet, EVOKES a theme and ECHOES a line of another sonnet, with its score. Cypher walks them like any graph.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.sonnetsIntro.de: Shakespeare's 154 sonnets are stored in Postgres, embedded into Qdrant, searched by meaning and grown into a graph. The question: which themes run through the sonnets, and where does Shakespeare echo himself? sonnets is the Postgres source. It has a row for each sonnet and for each of the 2,155 lines.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.sonnetsLines.de: The line table has a row for each of the 2,155 lines. The command embed_lines is a single governed SQL statement. Its embed() call turns each line's words into a vector, and the rows are written to Qdrant through the collection's write route.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.sonnetsSearch.d: lines_like is a search table. Provisa runs the search live in Qdrant, using the arguments your statement passes: here, a phrase and how many lines to return. Each line comes back with a score that says how close it is to the phrase.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.sonnetsThemeVie: Each theme view stores one fixed search, joined back to the lines it found, with each line's score. This one holds the twenty lines nearest to "the ravages of time"; four more hold beauty, mortality, jealousy and verse that outlives death.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.sonnetsThemesBy: For each theme, how many of the lines it found are in the Fair Youth sonnets and how many in the Dark Lady sonnets. Look for a theme that belongs to one sequence.
vectors is Qdrant. It holds one point for each line, and each point's vector is the embedding of that line's words. Provisa reads and writes it just as it does any other source.

🧭 This compass reopens the tour anytime. To leave, click the app or press Esc.

Provisa is one model that holds your data, its metadata and the processing between them. The same model defines your data estate and operates it, and it stays out of the data path.

That is why everything stays in sync, and why reuse is built in: a relationship, metric, mask or rule defined once serves every surface, environment and role. Duplicate tables and metrics, duplicate commands and rules, even two systems serving the same data sit side by side in the model, so duplication is easy to see and simple to remove.

It is compact, extensible and composable. It slots in beside what you have and brings order to the sprawl.

🎯 The core is one short exercise: connect a database, then query it in the language or tool you already use, or ask in plain English. About five minutes, right from your desktop, with no infrastructure to stand up.

zh/tour.json::tour.steps.step15.descript:
A relationship does two jobs. It shapes your data model: how tables across sources and domains connect, which every query surface follows, whether GraphQL nesting, Cypher paths or SQL joins.

It is also a rule. Joins are governed: a role without the ignore_relationships right can join only along registered relationships, so which ones exist decides which queries are legal. Grant that right deliberately to a role you trust and it joins freely (never in high-security mode).

Relationships link tables across sources, even across different databases, turning flat tables into a traversable graph.
