zh/tour.json::tour.steps.step20.descript:
🔧 Compose your whole delivery pipeline right here, with no separate ETL tool:
  • 👁️ Views: over any table, ephemeral or materialized, and views over views.
  • ⚡ Commands: governed, typed operations (an HTTP service, a Python model, a stored procedure) that do double duty: a step inside your pipeline, and a first-class API that downstream apps and agents call to act on your data, invokable from every surface, governed and traced.
  • ⭐ Entities & facts: declare a dimension or fact once and Provisa generates the warehouse, methodology-neutral: 3NF (Inmon), star schema (Kimball), or Data Vault.
  • 📏 Metrics: governed aggregate definitions (“net revenue”) with grain bound at query time. Define once, and every surface (SQL, GraphQL, AI agents) computes the same number, and views built on a metric regenerate when its definition changes.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.step20.title: Build your delivery pipeline
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.step21.descript:
🏗️ Materialize a view and you get a full ETL engine, declared, not scripted:
  • 📅 Scheduled snapshots on real business calendars: recurrence rules, holidays, business-day gating, and a close grace period, so it fires on your reporting calendar.
  • 🗄️ Store As…: replace, upsert, or keep history with snapshot / delta, plus incremental compute.
  • 🕰️ Time travel: bitemporal history; query the model as of any point in time.
  • ⚡ Near-real-time refresh with debounce, or freshness-driven republish as inputs change.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.step21.title: Materialize into a live warehouse
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.step22.descript:
🧬 Lineage is the dependency trail your derivations leave: what each view, calculated column or metric is built from, and what depends on it. This is a real query, analyzed: follow name_upper back through its transforms to the exact source columns that feed it.

Nothing runs; the query is only analyzed.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.step22.title: Lineage, end to end
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.step23.descript:
The Admin pages run the platform:
  • ⚙️ Choose and configure your federation engine: DuckDB (embedded, zero-config), Trino, PostgreSQL, ClickHouse, or a cloud warehouse as a first-class engine (Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, Microsoft Fabric, Azure Synapse). Swap it anytime; the model, the surfaces and the governance above it never change.
  • 🔗 Whichever engine you pick brings its own live external data reach: Parquet, Iceberg and Delta read in place, zero-copy, credentials provisioned for you. Anything it can't link live lands as a governed replica.
  • 🔑 Manage encryption keys and wire up auth providers
  • 📊 Full observability: redirect to any OpenTelemetry collector for enterprise-class trace management
  • 📤 Export the model's configuration, the whole model or chosen sections, as a file to review, diff and ship through CI/CD

The same model travels from local dev to production, validated at every step, with no rewrite:

  • Develop: embedded DuckDB, no Docker. Build & validate locally.
  • Validate at scale: Docker, spin up an engine + observability. Prove behavior against production engines.
  • Promote: point at your own infrastructure, build through CI/CD, ship to production.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.step23.title: Operate it
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.step3.descripti:
One picker lists every type, grouped by category: Subscriptions, RDBMS, Cloud DW, Analytics, Data Lake, NoSQL, Code Resolvers, Graph, File, API, Streaming, Enterprise, Data Quality, Other. Search by name or alias, or narrow with the category chips. Each type shows its logo and a reach icon: ⚡ read live in place, or a copy icon where Provisa reads a refreshed replica.

Pick one, fill the connection, Save.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.step3.title: 73 source types, 14 categories
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.step4.descripti:
Whatever the source, whether a Mongo collection, a Kafka topic, a REST endpoint or a graph, Provisa decomposes it into a 2D table: one uniform shape to query across every source.

📁 Group tables into domains, each owned by a data steward who guards the model's quality as it evolves.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.step4.title: Everything becomes a table
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.step5.descripti:
Choose a source, schema and table, then pick columns, each with its own policy:
  • 🎭 Masking: redact values per role
  • 👁️ Visibility: show or hide the column
  • 🏷️ Aliases: rename for the model

That's the whole setup: a source and a few tables. 🚀 Now let's query it. →
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.step5.title: Pick columns & policy
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.step6.descripti:
SQL lives in the SQL explorer. Standard SQL federated across every source: join Postgres to Mongo to a CSV in one statement. The model's own metadata and every activity trace are queryable tables here too, so you can join your audit log or lineage straight to live data.

🔌 The same governed SQL runs over several wire protocols besides this explorer; your tool picks the one it already speaks:

  • pgwire: every Postgres-compatible client (psql, DBeaver, Tableau, Power BI) connects out of the box.
  • JDBC: drops into any Java/JVM app, ETL pipeline or JDBC-capable BI tool.
  • Arrow Flight SQL: columnar streaming for ADBC clients, with no row re-encoding, built for large result sets.
  • DuckDB · airport: ATTACH Provisa from DuckDB and query the governed federation in place.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.step6.title: SQL (1 of 9 surfaces)
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.step7.descripti:
◈ The same query, typed as GraphQL:

{ inquiries { groupBy { user }, count } }

Grouping and aggregates over your relationships: 🎯 one endpoint, 📖 a self-documenting schema.

🔌 Call it from any GraphQL client, such as Apollo, Relay or urql. With federation enabled, Provisa joins an Apollo supergraph as a subgraph, so your federated model composes alongside your existing graphs.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.step7.title: GraphQL (2 of 9 surfaces)
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.step8.descripti:
🕸️ Traverse the federated model as a graph with Cypher:

MATCH (u:Users)-[:SUBMITTED]->(i:Inquiries)

↔️ That traversal runs across sources, with no single graph database required.

🔌 Any Bolt client, such as Neo4j Browser or Bloom, runs the same traversal over the wire, with no code change.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.step8.title: Cypher (3 of 9 surfaces)
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.step9.descripti:
⚙️ Every registered entity is also a gRPC service:

rpc QueryInquiries(...) returns (...)

Call it from any gRPC client: 📐 strongly typed, 🚀 high-throughput.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.step9.title: gRPC (4 of 9 surfaces)
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepBuildSource: That is how a source is added: the picker opened with its whole list, Parquet File was chosen, the file's address went in (supplies.parquet) and Save created it. The new supplies source reads that file in place.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepCache.descr: 🗄️ These layers are separate. The response cache holds query results, and a request opts in with @cached or a SQL comment. Small lookup tables are mirrored to speed joins. A replica of a source table that cannot be attached lives in the durable store, beside materialized views.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepCache.title: Caches and replicas
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepCommands.de: ⚡ A command is a governed, typed operation, such as an HTTP service, a Python model or a stored procedure. Register it once and call it from every surface, with the same rights and tracing as a query.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepDataProduct:
📦 Every product here speaks ODPS (the Open Data Product Standard): owner, team, purpose, limitations, usage, SLA, support and custom properties. Provisa publishes it straight into Snowflake Horizon and BigQuery Dataplex, so it shows up as a native product in the catalog your consumers already use.

🔁 There's no separate export step to forget: the spec is derived from the live model (tables, lineage, tags, ontology terms) every time, so what's published can't drift out of date the way a hand-maintained ODPS file would.

✅ Publishing also sends an ontology extract: the part of your ontology that bears on what is published: the terms that define its columns, the broader and related terms they connect to, and the typed relationships between them. The data-quality results of the checkers that scan it go with it. A product's Related Terms panel lists its terms.
Data products, published where consumers already look
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepDomains.des: 🗂️ A domain groups tables, and its data steward governs that part of the model: who sees what, masks and row rules, sensitive data, and its ontology and data products.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepEnvKinds.de: An environment is a branch of your model, and the list shows which environment each one was made from. When you create one, you choose its data. Inherit copies each source's connection from the parent, so the tables show the parent's data. Unbound, the default, gives you the whole model with no connections, and you point each source at your own database. Test (fake) reads the parent's rows through each column's fake, and Test (synthetic) reads rows generated from the parent's profile runs. A connection value that references a secret or an environment variable is copied as that reference, so rotating the credential reaches every environment that uses it.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepFakes.descr: 🎭 The Testing tab of a table's Columns shows each column's fake, such as email(). Fake only the identifying columns and keep the rest real. A column can also carry a synthetic rule, used only when generating synthetic data.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepFakes.title: Declare a fake
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepFakesFill.d: ✨ Fill from profile proposes fakes for identifying columns, and synthetic rules for the rest, from the table's latest profile. Nothing saves until you save the form.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepGlossary.de: 📖 Every term links to the columns that carry it and to other terms. Curate names, definitions, and typed relationships (kind-of, part-of, synonym-of) by hand, or let AI fill in the gaps from the ✨ menu: Definitions drafts only the terms still missing one, and Relationships proposes links across the whole ontology. Flag a term excluded from export to keep it out of published metadata.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepGlossaryTer: 📖 A term names one business concept, lists the columns that carry it, links to the terms it relates to and says what it means. Terms for real columns are derived for you; add one by hand for a concept no single column carries.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepMetrics.des: 📏 A metric is the business definition of a measure, an aggregate over one fact table. Define it once and SQL, GraphQL, the explore canvas and every view built from it compute the same number; a view regenerates when its metric changes.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepNotebook.de:
📓 The Notebook tab is JupyterLite: a Jupyter notebook running in your browser. Its first cell signs in, and the next reads the same statement as a DataFrame to chart or join with other data.

⬇️ Download the notebook and it opens in any desktop Jupyter, where the same cells read from Provisa as they do here.

One surface left: the one that writes your queries for you. →
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepObservabili: 🔭 Tracing records one span per request. The Debug tracing tab adds a span per pipeline stage and per source call, with SQL text. It adds load, so turn it on for one org, role or source for a set time; it turns itself off when the time is up.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepPolly.descr:
💬 Polly sets Provisa up in plain language.

“register my Postgres” · “fake the email column in the customers table” · “create a QA environment on synthetic data” · “who can see salaries?”

Polly works through the same governed APIs and rights as the UI, so it can only do what you can. Polly is open here; the chat button reopens this panel anytime.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepPolly.title: Meet Polly, your setup assistant
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepPreview.des: 👀 Expand a row and click Preview for live data through the governed pipeline: masked, access-controlled, and server-paged, so even a billion-row table opens instantly. Filters, sorts, and grouping run inside the query, and API-backed tables prompt for their required parameters first.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepProductForm: 📦 Name the owner and team, the purpose, usage, SLA and support, then pick the tables and commands it contains. These are the fields that get published. A table joins a product only when both share the same domain.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepProfilerChe: Every run adds rows to its result tables: per-column measures (null share, distinct count, range), per-run measures (row count), children per parent, quantiles and drift. Once you register a result table, a data-quality checker can scan it like any other table. That checker is a Soda or Great Expectations source, so any measure a profile produces can carry a check that raises an issue. Drift is one such measure. Each run is compared with the table's recent runs, and a measure that moves is flagged. From the profiler's runs you can add an accepted constraint, a drift check, or a check against expectations from outside Provisa to the checker's contract.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepPublish.des:
📤 Publish it where your org already looks. Catalog entries (tables, columns, domains, stewards, approved relationships), data products and column-level lineage go out, and each target receives what it supports: DataHub, OpenMetadata, Collibra, Atlan and Apache Atlas as catalogs, Snowflake Horizon and BigQuery Dataplex as data-product listings, and lineage over OpenLineage.

Publication is outbound only: Provisa never reads a target back as a source of truth.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepPublish.tit: Publish to the tools your org uses
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepPython.desc:
🐍 The Python tab runs Python in your browser, signed in as you:

provisa_client.query('SELECT species, COUNT(*) …')

The answer comes back as a pandas DataFrame, read through the same governed pipeline, so your role's row rules and masks apply to it too.

🔌 The same provisa-client package installs with pip on any desktop Python, so a script written here runs unchanged in your own environment.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepQualityPane: ✅ Write the contract by hand or build checks column by column (null rates, row counts, ranges, freshness) and dry-run it before saving. Every scan appends, so this table is the quality history: chart it, alert on it, join it to anything.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepQualityProd: ✅ A product's Data Quality panel lists the checker tables whose contracts scan its output ports, so a consumer sees the evidence next to the product. It is empty until a checker scans one. Data products are published in the Publish it Deep Dive.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepQualityProf: 📊 A Data Profiler is a source that profiles its member tables on a schedule. Add a table to one on the Quality tab of the table's editor. Each run measures every column's shape, distributions and most common values, and how many children each parent has. Run Profile Now starts a run, and View Profile Runs shows the results. The results land as tables that you register and govern like any other, and nobody sees a profile until you register them. The next card puts checks on them.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepQualityTabl: 🧪 A data-quality checker, Soda or Great Expectations, registers as a source. It scans back through Provisa's own postgres endpoint, so one contract dialect covers a Snowflake table, an Iceberg table and a Mongo collection alike. Its results land as an ordinary table: expand the row and open it like any other.
A quality checker is just a source
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepQuery.descr: 💬 You ask in the language or tool you already use (SQL, GraphQL, Cypher, plain language through Polly, or a BI tool or driver), and every one reads the same governed model, so the answer and the rules are the same whichever you pick.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepQuery.title: Query it your way
🤖 The model and its relationships are available to AI agents (Polly, and agents connecting over MCP), and they shape the queries those agents write.

An agent runs under a role, so the same rule applies to it as to a person: a query that joins outside the registered relationships fails. This is enforced, not advisory.

It is also your choice. To let an agent discover relationships, grant its role the ignore_relationships right; to keep it inside guardrails, leave the role without it. It is the same deliberate grant as for a trusted identity (never honored in high-security mode).
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepRelsList.de: 📋 Every relationship in the model, whether or not a source declares it. Filter and sort the list, and expand a row to edit a relationship or add its reverse. A role can join tables only along these relationships, unless it holds the ignore_relationships right.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepRelsSuggest: ✨ The sparkle button looks for likely joins: it reads the foreign keys your sources declare and, when an AI model key is configured, asks the model to infer more. Nothing is declared until you accept a candidate, and a rejected one stays out until you clear the rejections.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepReports.des: 📊 The audit log you queried earlier also feeds ready-made reports (usage ranking, PII access, policy denials, query health), each a governed view in the ops domain. Adding your own takes one SQL statement, and it becomes a cataloged, exportable data product like any other table.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepRequests.de: ✋ Someone who can't create relationships is asking to relate their tables to yours. They are often from another domain, and this is usually their first step toward asking for your data. Because relationships are governed, approving one changes which queries are legal: a role that may only join along approved relationships can now join across this one. A relationship request needs two approvals before it can run, and one that spans two domains needs a yes from each side. Approve it, run it, or reject it with a reason from a fixed list. Resolved requests move to the Resolved tab.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepRoleInherit: 👪 A role can inherit from a parent: it receives the parent's grants, column visibility and row rules, and its own row rule for a table replaces the parent's. The role also carries its capabilities and its rate and complexity limits.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepScheduled.d: ⏱️ Run a webhook, a SQL statement or a command on a cron schedule, when a table changes, or on a table's error or quarantine. A trigger runs as a role you choose, so governance applies, and each shows how its last run ended.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepSynthetic.d: 🧪 In the Synthetic data tab, define a dataset from the profile runs of the tables you name and press Generate. It fills a non-production environment with rows shaped like those tables, with the same relationships and fan-out, at the scale you choose. A comparison report shows how close it came.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepSyntheticPr: 🔒 Declare a dataset private with a privacy budget ε. Calibrated noise is added to every statistic the generator draws from a profile, and the report states what the noise dropped.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepTags.descri: 🏷️ A tag is one org-wide label with a fixed meaning, applied to sources, tables, columns, relationships or commands. Tags carry behavior, not only documentation, and a tag can require a reason, an expiry date or a parameter when it is applied.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepTags.title: Tags carry meaning
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepTestDataMap:
Safe, realistic data to build and test against comes from four parts, each with one job:

  • Environment: a branch of the model. At creation it inherits its parent's connections or starts unbound, and you point its sources at your own databases.
  • Profiler: measures real tables, giving the shapes everything else is built from.
  • Fakes: in test data, a column's fake replaces its identifying values.
  • Synthetic data: fills a non-production environment with generated rows shaped like the profiled tables.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.stepTestDataPro: 📊 A Data Profiler measures the tables you add to it: column shapes, distributions, value frequencies and children per parent. Fill from profile turns those measures into fakes, and a synthetic dataset draws its rows from them. Watching the same runs for drift is covered in the Data quality Deep Dive.
What fakes and synthetic data are built from
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.storefrontAnaly: The BI side reads as analyst: it sees every order, but no customer's email. Next, the run-as picker switches to analyst.
Late shipments by region and carrier, over the same tables and relationships. a_customer shows an email as the analyst reads it: masked.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.storefrontApp.d: This is the sample app's order-history screen, rendering that answer for the demo's signed-in customer: seven orders, their lines with product pictures from MongoDB, and delivery status from the shipping service. The app holds no joins and no access rules; the model holds both.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.storefrontAsCus: The app sends its queries as the customer role, whose row filters limit every answer to the signed-in customer's own orders. Next, the role picker switches to customer, so the query below runs just as the app runs it.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.storefrontBi.de: Apache Superset connects over the PostgreSQL wire protocol, with the PostgreSQL dialect: host and port of Provisa's pgwire server (5439 by default), database provisa, user analyst. It browses the shop's tables and views and charts revenue by region and late shipments by carrier from the same model.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.storefrontCatal: Each product is a MongoDB document, with its name, category, price and picture. Provisa reads it as a table.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.storefrontEvery: Next, the role picker switches back to All. The BI side reads as its own role, which is chosen where its SQL runs.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.storefrontJsonA: A client that prefers JSON:API asks for the same orders, still as the customer, with their lines and shipments included. Each order links the lines and the shipment it includes, and a line's id is its composite key.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.storefrontPoint: SHIPPED_AS joins an order to its shipment. The app and the BI tool both read through it and every other relationship, under the same rules: the customer sees their own orders, the analyst sees no emails. Change a relationship or a rule here, and both consumers have it. There is nothing to keep in sync.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.storefrontRelat: OF_PRODUCT joins an order line in PostgreSQL to its product in MongoDB. With PLACED_BY, HAS_ITEM and SHIPPED_AS, these four relationships are declared once, and both the app and the BI tool read through them.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.storefrontScena: A coffee retailer serves two consumers from one model. Its app's order-history screen shows a signed-in customer their orders, and its BI tool charts revenue and late shipments for the analysts. The orders are in PostgreSQL: customers, orders and each order's lines.
One model, an app and BI
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.storefrontScree: The order-history screen sends this one nested GraphQL query: each order with its lines, each line's product from the catalog, and the order's shipment from the shipping service. Run as customer, it answers seven orders, all the signed-in customer's own.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.storefrontShipp: Each order's shipment comes from the internal shipping service over REST, read through its OpenAPI document: the carrier, the tracking number, and when it was promised and delivered.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.streamingAnswer: orders_last_five_minutes is a materialized view of each region's orders and revenue over the last five minutes. Every batch of orders that lands refreshes it, so you're reading stored rows a few seconds old, never the topic itself. Run it again in a minute and the numbers will have moved.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.streamingCached: The same view in GraphQL. @cached(ttl: 10) asks for the response cache: the same question within ten seconds is answered from the cache, and the X-Provisa-Cache header says HIT.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.streamingCatalo: catalog is the shop's Postgres: what each product is and costs, and the regions the shop sells in.
The latest orders in the table, a few seconds behind the topic.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.streamingJoin.d: PLACED_IN joins each order to its region, and ORDERED to its product, so an order's revenue comes from the catalog's price.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.streamingLive.d: A GraphQL subscription on the orders: every batch that lands sends the latest orders again, as it lands. Leave it running and watch the list move.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.streamingOrders: orders is the topic, landed into its own table as the orders arrive. Every batch that lands refreshes the views that read it and notifies their subscribers.
A Kafka topic landed as a table and joined to the catalog. A view stayed current with every batch that landed. The same answer came back in SQL, GraphQL and REST, cached when asked, and a subscription followed the feed. Look around on your own from the query page.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.streamingRest.d: The same view as a REST call, for a dashboard that polls it.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.streamingScenar: A coffee shop's orders arrive on a Kafka topic, a few a second, and its catalog is in its Postgres. The question: which regions placed the most orders in the last five minutes? orders is the broker the orders arrive on.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.testdataCoverag: Before pre-prod existed, the coverage check listed every sensitive column and whether a fake covers it. Here customers.email has none. A Test (fake) environment refuses to open, and refuses every read, while a sensitive column has no fake. Once the steward declares one, the column is covered.
The same check, read now from the model: each sensitive column, its tags, and whether a fake covers it. Every one is covered, so pre-prod opens and answers.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.testdataDev.des: Every row in dev was generated from production's profile: the same columns, value shapes and spread, and none of the real rows. This is also the answer when even pre-prod's real rows can't leave production's boundary: give testers a synthetic copy.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.testdataDevAnsw: The same view in dev. The regions and categories are the ones production has, and the totals are close to production's without being its numbers.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.testdataDevGrap: Each order with the customer who placed it, through the relationship. Keys were generated to line up across tables, so every API reads dev as a consistent dataset.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.testdataDone.de: One model, three environments. Prod holds the real rows. Pre-prod reads them with every sensitive column faked, for every role. Dev is generated from production's profile and holds nothing real. Fakes are declared once per column, and an environment that would show a sensitive column unfaked refuses to open.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.testdataJoin.de: An order's customer_id and the customer's id are both faked as a hash. One real value always gives the same fake, so an order still finds its customer when both are fake.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.testdataPreprod: The same customers, read in preprod. Each name, email, city, sign-up date and customer number is a fake, computed as the row is read. The region is real. Pre-prod reads production's own data through Provisa, and the only identity that connects to production's stores is Provisa's own. Nothing is copied out.

The same view in preprod gives exactly production's revenue by region and category. Every real row, volume and edge case is there for final testing. The customer number is faked the same way on customers and on orders, so the joins still match.
As analyst, or as any other role, pre-prod's sensitive columns read as fakes. No grant, mask or role shows the real values in a Test (fake) environment.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.testdataProd.de: In prod you see the customers as they really are.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.testdataProdAns: Revenue by region and category, from the real orders.
The generation report compares each generated table with the production profile it was drawn from, column by column: distributions, null rates, distinct values and how columns move together. It shows how close dev is to production, without showing production.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.testdataScenari: shop-db is a shop's production database: customers, products and orders. Teams need data to build and test against. Here one model serves three environments. prod is the real rows, the source of truth, and nobody builds against it. preprod is production's own data with every sensitive column faked, for final testing. dev is generated from production's profile and holds nothing real, for everyday building.
Three environments over one production database
On customers, the name, email, city and sign-up date each declare a fake, and so does the customer number: an identifier, and the sign-up date a quasi-identifier that could single someone out. Region, products, orders and amounts declare none, so they stay real. Which columns to fake is the operator's choice, made once in the model.
The model says which columns are faked
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.testdataTest.de: A real value shows the same fake wherever it is read, so dev and test agree: a test written in dev finds the same rows in test.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.testdataToDev.d: Next, the switcher moves to dev, a Test (synthetic) environment.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.testdataToPrepr: Environments are branches of one model, as in git. Next, the switcher in the header moves to preprod, a Test (fake) environment.
Next, the switcher returns to prod.
Next, the switcher moves to test, the second Test (fake) environment.
zh/tour.json::tour.steps.vulnerabilities: One alert for each pinned package version with a published advisory: the repository, the package, the CVE, the version that fixes it, and whether the alert is open, fixed or dismissed.
The Dependabot alerts

The view exploited_in_our_code is stored. It keeps each open alert whose CVE is in CISA's catalog, with the number of days since CISA's due date passed. Internet-facing repositories come first, then the ones longest overdue. That's where to start.
The answer in SQL
The same view, grouped by team on the server: how many exploited vulnerabilities each team has open, and how long the oldest has been overdue.
The answer in GraphQL
The government data comes from AskAmerica: the NVD's CVE records, MITRE's catalog of software weaknesses and CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities.
The public vulnerability data
The same joins as a graph in Cypher: repositories, the open alerts raised in them, their CVEs and the catalog entries that mark them exploited.
The answer as a graph
A CVE record and its entry in CISA's catalog share the CVE identifier, and this relationship joins them. With the alerts joined to their CVEs, an alert reaches the catalog in two steps.
Exploited, by CVE
Each CVE that attackers are known to exploit, with the date federal agencies must fix it by and whether ransomware campaigns use it.
CISA's known exploited vulnerabilities

The NVD holds a quarter of a million CVEs, and the company's alerts name nineteen. The table's landing filter, a condition on its own columns, keeps only those when the table is landed, so the copy holds just the records the alerts need.
The CVE records, landed through a filter

zh/tour.json::tour.steps.worldcupFunctio:
country_alias is a Python source, and this function is the table every cross-source relationship joins through. It receives each team name the sources write, asks an LLM which FIFA member the name stands for, with a key from the organization's vault, and returns the member's name and FIFA code. It runs again on its refresh interval, so a new name is matched as it appears.
def country_alias(name: str) -> list[Alias]:
    """The FIFA member a team's name stands for: West Germany and Germany FR are Germany.

    @table
    """
    reply = anthropic.Anthropic().messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-5-5",
        max_tokens=2000,
        output_config={"effort": "low", "format": {"type": "json_schema", "schema": ANSWER}},
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": ASK + name}],
    )
    match = json.loads(next(b.text for b in reply.content if b.type == "text"))
    return [Alias(name, match["canonical_country"], match["fifa_code"])]
